To whoever unpacks their boxes here next,

I left the spare key inside the blue tin on the highest kitchen shelf—the one you can only reach if you stand on the edge of the counter, which I don’t recommend doing in socks. The landlord will tell you there isn’t a spare, mostly because he forgets things he doesn’t write on the back of envelopes, and because he has owned this building since 1984 and prefers to believe it runs on goodwill and radiator steam.

You should know a few things about Apartment 4B. None of them are in the lease.

First, the radiator in the bedroom is dramatic. Around five in the morning in January, it will knock three times—sharp raps, like someone knocking from the fire escape. The first winter I lived here, I stood in the dark holding a broomstick for twenty minutes before realizing it was just trapped air. Don’t bother bleeding the valve; it only makes it sulk. Give it five minutes, and it will settle into a low, steady hiss that eventually becomes the best white noise you have ever slept through.

Second, the floorboard just outside the bathroom door has a particular pitch. If you step on the left edge, it groans. If you step two inches to the right, it stays silent. You will learn this without meaning to. Within three months, your feet will navigate the dark on their own, memorizing the geometry of this place the way you memorize the pauses in a familiar song.

The light is the real reason I stayed six years. Wait until October. Around four-thirty, the sun clears the brick warehouse across the street and slips between the two sycamores. For about twenty minutes, the whole living room turns the color of steeped tea. Dust motes float in it like slow snow. If you have a chair you love, put it near the left window. Bring a book you don’t mind putting down. You won’t get much reading done during those twenty minutes anyway; the light asks too much of your attention.

Downstairs, in 3B, lives an elderly man named Arthur. He keeps odd hours and plays the cello. When I first moved in, he was terrible—just raw, scraping scales that vibrated straight up through the floorboards and into the soles of my shoes. I found out later he had broken his wrist in a fall and was teaching himself how to hold the bow again at seventy-two. By my second spring, the scales turned into Bach. By my fourth, I would sometimes lie flat on the rug just to feel the low notes humming against my ribs. If you run into him in the hallway, ask about his tomatoes. He grows them on his fire escape in buckets and will talk for fifteen minutes if you let him. Let him. In August, he leaves a paper bag of them by your door, still warm from the sun, tasting like nothing sold in a store.

Across the street, the corner bakery vents its ovens into the alley around four in the morning on Tuesdays and Fridays. If you sleep with the window cracked in the summer, cardamom and yeast will drift in before your alarm goes off. It is the gentlest way to wake up that I have ever known.

I suppose I should tell you why I’m leaving, since people always wonder what sort of luck is soaked into the walls of a new place.

Nothing bad happened here. Well—that isn’t quite true. Ordinary, difficult things happened here. A long relationship ended quietly at the kitchen table over two cups of cold coffee. A phone call came on a rainy Thursday in November with the kind of news that splits a life into *before* and *after*. There was a stretch where I ate toast over the sink and forgot to water the ferns.

If you look closely at the molding by the front door, you can still see a faint pencil mark where I measured my nephew’s height the summer he turned five, and another two inches higher the year after. I painted over most of the scuffs before I packed, as the lease requires, but I left those two lines. You can paint over them if you want. I just couldn’t quite bring myself to erase them.

Mostly, though, this apartment held me together while I figured out who I was going to be next. It was small enough that I couldn’t hide from myself, and bright enough that I didn’t want to. I learned to cook actual dinners on that uneven gas stove—the back right burner runs hot, by the way, so never trust it with garlic. I learned to sit alone on a Saturday night without feeling like I was waiting for someone to arrive. One April, I fell in love again, unexpectedly, on the front stoop while waiting for a locksmith because I had locked myself out in the rain. That’s why I’m leaving, actually. We found a place with a yard and a kitchen wide enough for two people to chop onions together.

The rooms look strangely hollow right now. Without rugs and books, every footstep echoes, and the air smells faintly of lemon cleaner and cardboard. It feels like leaving behind a coat that finally fits my shoulders.

Be patient with the front lock; lift the handle slightly as you turn the key. Don’t trust the back right burner. Listen for the cello when the weather turns cool.

I hope the light finds you in October. I hope you fill these rooms with loud dinners, quiet mornings, and the kind of ordinary days you only realize were golden years after they’ve passed.

Welcome home.
